lines: Every earlier topic in this chapter answered one question: given a row, how do you find it fast.
Here's a different question. Two transactions reach for that exact same row at the exact same moment.
What does a third transaction, just trying to read, see while that's happening?
I updated one row on a real cluster, then asked Postgres directly what's sitting on that page right now.
Not one tuple. Two — the one from before the update, and the one from after, both still physically there.
Watch the transaction number. It closes the old tuple and opens the new one — the same number, in two different fields.
That header alone can't tell a reader whether a tuple counts.
A reader also carries its own snapshot — a record of which transactions were still running when it started — and for anything outside that list, there's one more question: did it actually commit.
Two checks, not one, before a version is considered visible at all.
InnoDB and Oracle don't keep two tuples around like that.
Each row has exactly one physical copy on disk, and a plain update changes it right where it sits.
So a reader who needs the value from a moment ago — where does that come from, if there's only one copy left?
answer: Not by waiting. That's the assumption locking-era databases made, and it isn't what either system does here.
Both keep a separate log of exactly what got overwritten.
A reader who needs the old value doesn't get a second tuple handed to it — it gets that log, rebuilt into a readable version.

lines: Same update, this time under that other model, straight from each engine's own documentation.
The row itself: one copy, changed in place. Nothing duplicated there.
Off to the side, a record of exactly what it used to say — structurally nothing like what you just watched Postgres do.
An append-only design has to pay for itself somewhere. Here's where.
I updated the same row, over and over, on a column that's indexed, with nothing running to clean up behind it.
The table grew. The index grew. Every one of those old tuples is still sitting there, because nothing has told Postgres it's safe to reuse that space yet.
This is the payoff for all of that.
One connection opens a transaction and reads a value. A second, completely separate connection updates and commits that same row while the first is still open.
The first connection reads again. Same answer. Not delayed, not blocked — its own snapshot from a few steps back is exactly what makes that possible.
That bounded log from a few steps back has a sharp edge.
It's reused in a circle — new undo eventually overwrites old undo, because the space isn't infinite.
A reader that's still running when its own undo gets overwritten doesn't get a stale answer. It gets no answer at all — that's what snapshot too old actually means.
Step back and look at what you've actually seen.
Postgres pays as it goes — every write leaves something behind, and the next topic is exactly what deals with that.
The other family pays differently — cheap writes in place, reconstruction work on long reads, and one hard limit that Postgres, structurally, doesn't share.
One more scenario, worth working through before the answer lands.
A team keeps hitting that failure on a nightly report and turns one dial to make it stop: more retention.
Does that actually fix what's wrong, or does it just buy some time?
answer: It buys time. The underlying shape of the problem hasn't moved.
Retention, by Oracle's own description, is a target the database tries for — not a promise.
Give it more room and the report runs longer before failing again. Grow the writes instead, and the exact same failure comes back.
